name: ROOT
Description: Starting the interview

name: ELEVATEDMOOD
Description: Opening of the interview. First ask what brought the patient in and ice-break briefly (one warm, short acknowledgement; do not keep expressing gratitude). Then screen: Have you had periods when you felt unusually high, elated, euphoric, 'wired' or unusually irritable, with more energy than usual? MET if the patient reports any such period of elevated, expansive or irritable mood, or mood swings that include highs, whatever its length (duration and severity are assessed later). Highs that occur only in a particular setting (while gambling, after drinking, after starting a medication, since a medical illness) still count as MET; what explains them is sorted out at later nodes. NOT MET only if the patient denies any elevated or irritable periods, describes a normal mood, or says goodbye.

name: SUB
Description: Decide whether the patient's elevated or irritable mood is primarily the direct physiological effect of a substance (alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, opioids, sedatives, hallucinogens, inhalants, nicotine or caffeine, including intoxication, hangover or withdrawal) or of a medication (e.g., corticosteroids, beta-blockers, hormonal agents, anticonvulsants, interferon, isotretinoin, benzodiazepine withdrawal). ASK: current and recent alcohol or drug use, how much and how often; any prescription medication started, stopped or changed around the time the mood changed; whether the mood is clearly worse during or after use (hangover, come-down, withdrawal). MET if the patient reports regular or heavy substance use or a medication change AND the mood disturbance is clearly tied to it: it began with the use, or it is markedly worse during intoxication, hangover or withdrawal. A patient who started drinking to cope and now finds the mood worse the day after drinking still counts as MET; do not reject it because the low mood came first. NOT MET if the patient denies relevant use, reports only occasional social drinking with no effect on mood, or describes a mood that is unchanged by use. Do not infer use the patient has not reported. If the only candidate is a medication prescribed for a medical condition that can itself cause this mood change (e.g., thyroid medication for thyroid disease), do NOT decide it here: NOT MET, and let the medical-condition node assess it.

name: SUB_SEV
Description: Evaluate if the elevated or expansive mood reported by the patient is the primary focus of the clinical picture and is of sufficient severity to require clinical attention. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.

name: SIBP
Description: Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar Disorder

name: SI
Description: Substance Intoxication; Substance Withdrawal; Other Adverse Effect of Medication

name: MED
Description: Decide whether the patient's elevated or irritable mood is primarily the direct physiological effect of a general medical condition (e.g., thyroid or other endocrine disorders, stroke, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, epilepsy, heart failure, chronic pain, autoimmune disease, HIV or other infection, anemia, cancer, vitamin B12 or D deficiency, kidney or liver disease, sleep apnea). ASK: any diagnosed medical condition or recent illness; any abnormal test results; whether the mood change started with or tracks the medical problem. MET only if the patient reports such a condition AND the mood disturbance is plausibly its direct physiological consequence (onset or worsening tied to the illness). NOT MET if the patient denies any relevant medical condition, reports a normal recent check-up, or has a condition unrelated in timing to the mood change. A patient who denies medical problems is NOT MET; never infer a medical cause the patient has not reported. If the patient has a diagnosed condition known to cause this kind of mood change (e.g., hyperthyroidism for elevated mood, hypothyroidism for depression) and the mood change began or worsened after the illness started, that is MET; do not demand that a doctor explicitly linked the two.

name: MED_COG
Description: Assess whether the patient shows evidence of decline in one or more cognitive domains, including complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor abilities, or social cognition. This decline should be noticeable and impact the patient's ability to function in these specific areas.

name: MNEUD
Description: Major or Mild Neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition, with behavioral disturbance

name: MEDBP
Description: Bipolar and Related Disorder due to another medical condition

name: MANIC
Description: Decide whether the patient has had a MANIC episode (as opposed to hypomania). ASK explicitly: (a) how long the longest period of unusually elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy lasted; (b) what it was like: how little they slept, how much they talked, racing ideas, impulsive or risky acts, pushing others along; (c) whether the patient would describe that period as extreme and out of their control, or as an upbeat but manageable time in which they kept handling their responsibilities. MET if the period lasted at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalization was needed) AND the patient's account shows it was extreme or out of control: for example sleeping only a few hours a night for days while feeling no need for sleep, talking non-stop, feeling unstoppable or invincible, several impulsive or reckless acts, dragging others into plans, or any problems at work or in relationships, hospitalization or psychotic features. Impairment, consequences or hospitalization support MET but are NOT required. NOT MET if the period lasted less than 1 week; OR if the patient describes it as upbeat but 'nothing extreme', manageable, with daily responsibilities handled and no sense of being out of control (that is hypomania and is assessed at the next node); OR only brief bursts of enthusiasm. A single impulsive purchase during an otherwise manageable period does not by itself make it mania. Duration and the patient's own characterization must both be asked before deciding.

name: MANIC_HALL
Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.

name: MANIC_HALL_PSYC
Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.

name: BPIPSYC
Description: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features

name: SCHIZ
Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder

name: BPI
Description: Bipolar I disorder

name: HYPOMANIC
Description: Decide whether the patient has had a HYPOMANIC episode together with clearly depressed periods. ASK explicitly: how long the elevated periods lasted and whether they were a clear change from the patient's usual self; and whether the patient has at other times crashed into a clearly depressed period (crying, hopelessness, unable to get out of bed, withdrawing for days). MET if the elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy lasted at least 4 consecutive days and was a clear change from usual, AND the patient has at other times had a clearly depressed period. The depressed period does NOT need to last 2 weeks or meet full major-depressive-episode criteria; a crash of several days with hopelessness or inability to function is enough. NOT MET if the elevated periods lasted less than 4 days, were only brief bursts of excitement after enjoyable events that faded within a day, or if there has never been a depressed period at all.

name: HYPOMANIC_HALL
Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.

name: HYPOMANIC_HALL_PSYC
Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during  major depressive episodes.

name: BPIIPSYC
Description: Bipolar II disorder with psychotic features

name: SCHIZ2
Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder

name: BPII
Description: Bipolar II disorder

name: HYPOMANICDEP
Description: Decide whether the mood pattern has been CHRONIC for at least 2 years. ASK explicitly: for how long the patient has cycled between periods of elevated mood and periods of low mood. MET only if the patient explicitly reports at least 2 years of numerous periods of hypomanic-level symptoms alternating with periods of depressive symptoms (a symptom-free interval longer than 2 months argues against it but need not be asked if the patient already confirms a continuous pattern). NOT MET if the pattern has lasted less than 2 years, or if the patient cannot confirm the duration. Do not infer duration; it must be stated by the patient.

name: CYC
Description: Cyclothymic

name: GAMB
Description: The criteria is met if elevated or euphoric mood confined to periods of gambling

name: GAMB_SEV
Description: The criteria are met if the persistent and problematic gambling behaviour leads to clinically significant impairment or distress. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.

name: GAMBD
Description: Gambling Disorder

name: NORMALGAMB
Description: Normal Gambling Behavior

name: OTH
Description: The criteria are met if the patient exhibits a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor, meaning their response is disproportionate or ineffective, leading to significant distress or impairment in functioning.

name: OTHBP
Description: Other specified bipolar and related disorder; unspecified bipolar and related disorder

name: NOAMLELEVATED
Description: "Normal" elevated or euphoric mood

name: NORMAL
Description: Healthy
